edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina (PL 1, Paris 1844), De baptismo, via Latin Wikisource transcription
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Exinde, egressi de lavacro, perungimur benedicta unctione de pristina disciplina, qua ungi oleo de cornu in sacerdotium solebant. Ex quo Aaron a Moyse unctus est: unde Christus dicitur, a chrismate quod est unctio, quae Domino nomen accommodavit, facta spiritualis, quia spiritu unctus est a Deo Patre, sicut in Actis: Collecti sunt enim vere in ista civitate adversus sanctum Filium tuum, quem unxisti. Sic et in nobis carnaliter currit unctio, sed spiritaliter proficit: quomodo et ipsius Baptismi carnalis actus, quod in aqua mergimur; spiritalis effectus, quod delictis liberamur.
pass_a_gloss: From there, having come out from the bath, we are anointed with blessed anointing from the former discipline, by which they were accustomed to anoint with oil from the horn into the priesthood. From which Aaron was anointed by Moses: whence Christ is called, from the chrism which is anointing, which accommodated the name to the Lord, made spiritual, because He was anointed with the Spirit by God the Father, as in the Acts: For they were gathered together indeed in this city against Your holy Son, whom You anointed. So also in us the anointing runs carnally, but profits spiritually: just as also the bodily act of that very Baptism, which is that we are immersed in water; the spiritual effect, which is that we are freed from sins.

bible_refs.note: Collecti sunt enim vere in ista civitate adversus sanctum Filium tuum, quem unxisti

pass_b_english: After leaving the baptismal bath, we receive a blessed anointing that comes from an ancient practice: in the old days, priests were anointed with oil from a horn. That custom goes back to Aaron, whom Moses anointed. The very name 'Christ' comes from 'chrism,' meaning anointing — the title fits the Lord because He was anointed spiritually, by the Spirit from God the Father, just as Acts says: 'They were truly gathered together in this city against Your holy Son, whom You anointed' (Acts 4:27). In us, too, the anointing is applied physically, but its benefit is spiritual — exactly like baptism itself: the bodily act is immersion in water; the spiritual effect is freedom from sins.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A preserves the clause structure and nuances (e.g., 'carnally runs' vs 'applied physically'). Pass B provides a fluent rendering that maintains the theological distinctions. The scripture citation (Acts 4:27) is correctly identified and added in Pass B as required.
